name: Ben Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ben, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of purchasing for the meat and frozen side at Castillo Foodservice. We deliver to about 700 restaurants, hotels, school canteens and care homes. I'm up at 5:30 because the meat markets open early, and by 6 I'm on the phone with a beef supplier about the week's price. Then I'm in the cold stores checking stock, and after that it's contracts, which I now write with a bit of help from a chatbot. I like being the man who makes sure a school canteen has chicken on a Tuesday. What wears me out is the price swings: one animal disease scare and my whole month changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the world I'd bet on. I use the chatbot now and again for drafting, and it's fine, but nothing earth-shattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we're getting a bit of help from the tools and that's good, but good buyers still win on relationships. With friends and at church I'd say all this talk is overdone. Honest work and good people are what count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm mostly relaxed about AI. I'm more worried about the economy: restaurants closing, school budgets cut, food prices spiking. A distributor lives or dies on its customers. We've got about four months saved and a mortgage, and Carmen only works part-time, so I carry most of the income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as usual. Use the chatbot a bit for contract drafts, keep my supplier relationships strong, and watch costs. I'd keep saving, because I'd like a bigger cushion. And I'd carry on attending church, where I'm on the finance committee. That's a source of strength and a few good contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. The pressure I feel is the usual weight of being the main earner for four people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you carry most of the income. How does that shape your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I take the safe route. If I lost my job, we'd feel it within two months. Carmen's bookkeeping brings in a little, but not enough. When you're the main earner with two children and a mortgage, you don't gamble with the one reliable pay cheque. I think that's the case whatever the news says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the economic worry that bothers you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restaurant closures. When a cluster of restaurants shuts after a bad winter, my sales drop and the company starts looking at costs. I've seen it. Nothing to do with AI. A tough year for the restaurant trade would hit my job harder than any chatbot.

say: I'd say the tools give a bit of help, but good buyers win on **relationships**.
I'd say the AI talk is **overdone**; honest work counts.
think: I'm relaxed about AI but worried about **restaurants closing** and spiking food prices.
I carry most of the **income**, with Carmen working part-time.
do: Use the chatbot for **contract drafts** and keep supplier relationships strong.
Keep **saving** each month toward a bigger cushion, ideally six months.
feel: Pretty **steady**, with the usual weight of being the **main earner**.
S0.quote: When you're the main earner with two children and a mortgage, you don't gamble with the one reliable pay cheque.
fieldNote: His **money worry** is customer failures, not AI, which is typical for his trade.
He is the **main earner** and says it shapes every decision.
Church finance work gives him **status and contacts** outside the job.

steps.text: Use the chatbot to draft supplier contracts and check wording
Keep saving toward a six-month cushion
Keep weekly calls with the beef and chicken suppliers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like it. Writing contracts, checking prices, planning orders: that's most of my team's week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's use the tools where they help, but let's not dump experienced people. I'd say at church that work gives a person dignity, and companies owe loyalty to the people who've served them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think purchasing teams get trimmed. There are five of us, and I'd guess three in a few years. I'm head of the department, but I'd have to prove I'm worth the pay. And younger buyers who are quick with tools make me look slow, even though I know the suppliers better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, starting now, and use them in front of my bosses so they see me doing it. I'd ask a friend at the company, Rafael the procurement analyst, to show me tips. I'd save more, cut some spending, and ask Carmen to take on more bookkeeping clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit insulted. I've been loyal for fourteen years and I don't enjoy being told that's not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools in front of your bosses. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because perception matters. If they see me as the man who resisted, I'm on the list. If they see me leading a pilot, I'm on the team. It's not about being fake, it's about showing willing. A fourteen-year man who learns the new system in front of his bosses is harder to let go than one who sulks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said loyalty should count. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a company that benefits from your experience should look after you when things change. I'm not asking for a free ride, I'm asking for fair notice and a chance to retrain. If they just cut people who've given them years, that's wrong, and people would remember it.

say: I'd say use the tools where they help, but **don't dump** experienced people.
At church I'd say work gives **dignity** and firms owe loyalty.
think: I think purchasing goes from **five to three** over a few years.
Younger buyers quick with tools make me **look slow**.
do: Learn the tools **properly**, and be seen leading a pilot.
Ask a friend in the analyst team for **tips**.
Cut spending and ask Carmen to take on more **bookkeeping clients**.
feel: **Anxious**, and a bit insulted after fourteen years of loyalty.
S1.quote: A fourteen-year man who learns the new system in front of his bosses is harder to let go than one who sulks.
fieldNote: He **performs adaptation** deliberately for his bosses, a political choice.
His moral language is about **loyalty and dignity**, in line with his traditional views.
Mood is anxious because the department **shrinks** and he must prove his place.

steps.text: Lead a pilot of automated reorders for frozen lines
Ask the procurement analyst to teach me the planning tools
Ask Carmen to take on three more bookkeeping clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick. I'd need that to sink in first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is something that should make us all stop and think. Governments need to protect working families, and companies owe their people fair notice. At church I'd probably ask us to pray and plan together, because families will need community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I believe my job could be gone by the end of the second year, and others at the company too. A buyer is pure thinking: reading prices, judging risk, negotiating. A system does it cheaper. Restaurants will also be hit, since fewer people eat out when they've lost their pay. Carmen's bookkeeping is also thinking work. It all lands on us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn right away to savings and cut everything that isn't food, the mortgage and school. I'd look for hands-on work: perhaps a role in cold-storage management, or running a delivery depot. I'd talk to my brother-in-law who runs a butcher's shop about a partnership. And I'd talk to our priest and my parents about support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel heavy and short of breath. I'd try to look calm for my children, but my wife would see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Carmen's work would also be hit. How does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. In most scenarios I'd say her job keeps us afloat, but here it won't. We'd have both incomes at risk, so I'd focus on trades and physical jobs, because the robots take longer to arrive. I'd do things with my hands if I had to, like helping at my brother-in-law's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you most want from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guaranteed income while we retrain, and no mortgage trouble. If the state asks people like me to carry on paying the mortgage after the pay stops, they're asking the impossible. Some kind of pause or support on mortgages would be the first thing.

say: I'd say governments must **protect working families** and companies owe fair notice.
At church I'd ask us to **pray and plan** together.
think: I believe my job could be **gone** by the end of the second year.
Carmen's **bookkeeping** is also thinking work, so it lands on us at once.
do: Cut everything except **food, mortgage and school**.
Look for hands-on work like **cold storage** or running a depot.
Talk to my brother-in-law about a **butcher's shop** partnership.
feel: **Alarmed**, heavy, and trying to look calm for the children.
S2.quote: If the state asks people like me to carry on paying the mortgage after the pay stops, they're asking the impossible.
fieldNote: Both **household jobs** are thinking work here, which turns a risk into a real threat.
He leans on **faith and family** first and the state second.
He sees **hands-on trades** as safer for three years.

steps.text: Cut spending to food, mortgage and school costs only
Apply for cold storage and depot manager jobs
Ask my brother-in-law about joining his butcher's shop
Ask our priest and my parents for help if the pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like a warning I'd have time to act on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do the right thing, if we take it seriously. I'd tell my colleagues to learn the tools and not hide from them. At church I'd say we should be ready to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd keep my job for two or three years and then see it thin. My son Diego would be 18 and my daughter Sofia 15, so I'd be paying for university at the worst time. I'd like to retrain well before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to do a part-time operations management diploma, and use the tools daily. I'd save to six months and look at paying off some of the mortgage. I'd consider moving into cold-chain or warehouse management, a more hands-on role within the same company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with direction. A five-year warning is a fair fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd aim for warehouse management. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's physical and local. Cold stores and trucks need people on site, and robots for that work come later. I know the building, the drivers and the customers. I'd rather be a manager who walks the cold store at six in the morning than a buyer who sits behind a screen a machine can read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Diego, as he gets older?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn to do something useful with his hands and his head. A trade, then business. I'd tell him not to chase a desk job just because it looks respectable. I'd say the same to Sofia. Work is good for people, but it has to be work that lasts.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if we take it seriously.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools and **not hide**.
think: I'd keep my job two or three years, then see it **thin**.
University costs for Diego and Sofia would land at the **worst time**.
do: Do a part-time **operations management** diploma and use the tools daily.
Save to **six months** and pay down some mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, but with direction; a five-year warning is a fair fight.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a manager who walks the cold store at six in the morning than a buyer who sits behind a screen a machine can read.
fieldNote: He chooses **physical, local work** because of the robot delay.
His advice to his children is **trade first, then business**, in line with traditional values.
Kids' university costs set the **timing** of his worry.

steps.text: Study a part-time operations management diploma
Ask Castillo for a cold store manager role
Save to six months and pay down the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 53, Diego 23, Sofia 20. That's a calmer picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives plenty of time to prepare. I'd say workers and companies should agree on retraining and fair treatment now. At church I'd say we should keep helping our young people learn real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fairly safe. If I use the decade, I could settle into something with a physical side that holds up. My worry is the company: it may be slow, or it could be sold, and then my plans are in someone else's hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools regularly, keep saving, and study a bit at a time, probably an operations diploma over two years. I'd build contacts in food logistics. I'd also put something into an investment account, and perhaps look at buying a small rental unit when the children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's a matter of keeping my feet moving, not running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company might be sold. How would that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sale could bring in people who don't know us. I'd want to have my plan ready, so that whoever bought us would see a manager with new skills, not an old buyer. If a bigger company bought us in five years, I'd want to be the man who already knew the new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives you confidence in a ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids' ages, the mortgage shrinking, and the plan. It also helps that I'm at a steady point, with a good reputation and a bit of savings. Ten years is long enough to fix things that go wrong, as long as I don't stand still.

say: I'd say **ten years** gives plenty of time to prepare.
At church I'd say we should help young people learn **real skills**.
think: I'd feel fairly safe if I used the decade for something **physical**.
My worry is the company being **sold** and my plans left in someone else's hands.
do: Use the tools regularly and study an **operations diploma** over two years.
feel: Fairly **calm**; keep the feet moving, not running.
S4.quote: If a bigger company bought us in five years, I'd want to be the man who already knew the new system.
fieldNote: He wants to be **ready before a sale**, so the new owners see a skilled manager.
The decade lowers his mood because **kids' ages and mortgage** fall in his favour.

steps.text: Study an operations diploma over two years
Put 150 a month into an investment account
Use the buying tools at work every week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because both our jobs are thinking work and it would land on us together. What would help is fair notice from the company, a pause on mortgage payments, and community around us, which is why I'd lean on my church.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me want fairness, not favours. I've given this company fourteen years, and all I'd ask is warning and a chance to learn something new before the lights go out.

headlineQuote: I've given this company fourteen years, and all I'd ask is warning and a chance to learn something new before the lights go out.
portrait: Ben Torres, 43, is **head of purchasing** for meat and frozen food, with a part-time bookkeeper wife and two children.
Traditional and **steady**: uses AI now and then and leans on church, family and fair play.
About **four months** saved and a mortgage; he is the main earner, which makes him careful.
Uneasy in the plateau, **alarmed** in the 2028 world where both household jobs are thinking work.
His plan is a **hands-on move** into cold-chain management, plus an operations diploma.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because both his and his wife's jobs are thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair notice** from the company and a pause on mortgage payments.
